newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Indians, Pakistanis see mixed 50 years.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Indians, Pakistanis see mixed 50 years.

text.p: As India and Pakistan celebrated 50 years of independence, their overseas diaspora in London reflected with a mix of pride and sorrow on Thursday on a half century of achievement and disappointment.
For Indians the golden jubilee is an occasion for pride in building the world's largest democracy and winning freedom from British rule without war.
For Pakistanis the pride comes in establishing an independent, Islamic homeland and defying predictions that such a country would never survive on its own.

But for both groups these triumphs are tinged with regret at what might have been -- regret that the two states have not broken out of their vicious cycle of poverty, regret that they remain implacable enemies.

"When we live together peacefully here, respect each other's views, why the hell can't we solve our problems over there?" asked 63-year-old Braji-mohen Gupta, a Delhi native who now owns the Chaat House restaurant in London's Southall neighbourhood.

This bustling corner of southwest London has been dubbed by locals the mini-Punjab after the border district split between India and Pakistan a half century ago when Britain partitioned the colony into two nations on August 15, 1947.

"India and Pakistan spend billions and billions in an armaments race with nuclear weapons. What is the point if the people don't even have the basics like drinking water or decent housing? We must raise our voices and say enough is enough," Gupta said as he directed kitchen workers with confident hand movements.
Sixty-year-old Gurdip Gujral, a Punjab native, filled with reproach when asked about independence: "India has achieved nothing in 50 years, only corruption. It has so much potential."
Southall has been a confluence of immigrants from the I Indian subcontinent, with nearly 23,000 ethnic Indians and more than 3,000 Pakistanis and Bangladeshis.
Corner shops teem with rich fruits, spices and nuts from the subcontinent -- split peas, fresh coriander and curry leaves, green and red chillies, dried limes and ground mangoes.
Despite the relative harmony between the Pakistani and Indian communities in Southall, the two groups differed sharply over the issue of partition and creation of an Islamic state.
Ayaz Jahanzaib, a Pakistani who works at the Kashmiri Restaurant on Southall's high street, grew animated as he spoke of his country's creation.

"It was the first time in history that a country was created on the basis of its faith. We Moslems have our own identity, our own country," he explains. "We could never have been accommodated in India. Moslems have a very different way of life from Hindus."
But then the 47-year-old from outside Islamabad began to shake his head, adding wistfully:

"After 50 years we are not where we should be. Pakistan has had only a few sincere leaders. The others just feathered their own nests. The younger generation, we see that people don't have their basic rights. Obviously, that is a great disappointment."

Outside the restaurant's doorway the latest hits in Indian and Pakistani rock music pulse through the streets, while store after store offers highly stylised traditional costumes, pyjamas and reams of patterned sari fabrics.
At one of the nearby music shops an employee, a Delhi native who recently moved to London, criticised Pakistan for over-emphasising religion.

"We live as one big family in India. We have so many religions peacefully under one roof. But there are so many fanatics over there, so many problems," she said, quickly adding that she did not want to be named.
"We had no other choice but partition. But we in India did not want it. It didn't have to happen."
At the Bhai Bhai Housewives Cash & Carry, Tharakrar Narendra, an Indian who came to Britain 25 years ago from Uganda, said cleaving the subcontinent in two had only brought problems.
"If Pakistan and India were together they would be the biggest power in the world. That would be something. They are both religious countries, and that means they are warm-hearted."
